content: The invention of the sphygmomanometer is credited to Samuel Siegfried Karl Ritter von Basch. In 1896, Scipione Riva-Rocci, an Italian physician, introduced a more user-friendly version of the device. Later, in 1901, Harvey Cushing, an American neurosurgeon, discovered and popularized its use. A typical sphygmomanometer includes an inflatable cuff, a measuring unit (such as a mercury manometer), a connecting tube, and, in non-automatic models, an inflation bulb. The cuff is inflated until the artery beneath it is completely occluded. There are two main types of sphygmomanometers: 1. Digital Sphygmomanometers: These are electronic devices that are easy to use and practical in noisy environments. However, many digital models have not been validated for all patient populations and may provide inaccurate readings. Digital oscillometric monitors are not suitable for certain conditions, such as arteriosclerosis, arrhythmias, preeclampsia, pulsus alternans, and pulsus paradoxus. 2. Manual Sphygmomanometers: These are considered more traditional and precise but require operation by a trained individual. For this reason, they are often used in clinical trials and for evaluating high-risk patients, such as pregnant women. Examples of sphygmomanometers include mechanical devices with aneroid manometers and stethoscopes, as well as mercury manometers.
